q: Which condition must hold for an object to move with simple harmonic motion?
options: Its acceleration is constant and directed towards equilibrium
Its acceleration is proportional to its displacement and directed towards equilibrium
Its acceleration is proportional to its displacement and directed away from equilibrium
Its speed is proportional to its displacement from equilibrium
why: SHM needs $a = -\omega^2 x$: acceleration proportional to displacement, and the minus sign means it always points back towards equilibrium.

q: An oscillator has angular frequency $\omega = 10\pi$ rad $\text{s}^{-1}$. What is its period in seconds?
A simple pendulum is replaced by one four times as long. By what factor does its period change?
why: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$, so $T$ depends on $\sqrt{l}$: four times the length gives twice the period, not four times.

q: Where is the kinetic energy of a mass on a spring, oscillating with simple harmonic motion, greatest?
options: Halfway between equilibrium and maximum displacement
It is the same at every point
why: Speed is greatest as the mass passes through equilibrium. At maximum displacement it is momentarily at rest, so all the energy is potential there.

q: A particle moves with SHM with $\omega = 5.0$ rad $\text{s}^{-1}$ and amplitude 0.030 m. What is its maximum speed in $\text{m s}^{-1}$?
why: Maximum speed is at $x = 0$: $v = \omega x_0 = 5.0 \times 0.030 = 0.15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

q: A particle obeys $x = x_0 \sin(\omega t + \phi)$. At $t = 0$ it is at $x = -x_0$. Which phase angle $\phi$ fits?
why: We need $\sin\phi = -1$, so $\phi = 3\pi/2$. $\phi = \pi/2$ gives $x = +x_0$, and $\phi = 0$ or $\pi$ start at equilibrium.

q: How do the particles of the medium move as a longitudinal wave passes?
options: They oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer
They oscillate perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
They travel along with the wave at the wave speed
They move in circles around their equilibrium positions
why: In a longitudinal wave the particles oscillate back and forth along the direction the wave travels. They do not travel with the wave: only energy is transferred.

q: A wave on a rope has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 0.40 m. What is its speed in $\text{m s}^{-1}$?
why: $v = f\lambda = 50 \times 0.40 = 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

q: A sound wave passes from air into water. Which quantity stays the same?
why: Frequency is set by the source, so it does not change. The speed in water is higher, so the wavelength increases ($\lambda = v/f$).

q: Which of these waves cannot travel through a vacuum?
why: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium. Radio waves, X-rays and gamma rays are all electromagnetic waves, which travel through a vacuum.

q: A sound of frequency 680 Hz travels through air at $340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. What is its wavelength in metres?
Which list of electromagnetic waves is in order of increasing wavelength?
why: From short to long wavelength: gamma, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio. The first list is in decreasing order.

q: Water waves pass from deep into shallow water, where they travel more slowly. What happens?
why: Frequency is fixed by the source and never changes on refraction. With a lower speed, $\lambda = v/f$ must decrease.

q: A transparent material has refractive index 2.0. What is the critical angle, in degrees, for light inside it meeting a boundary with air ($n = 1.0$)?
why: At the critical angle the refracted ray is at 90°: $\sin c = 1.0/2.0 = 0.50$, so $c = 30°$.

q: Two coherent sources oscillate in phase. At a point P the path difference from the sources is $1.5\lambda$. What happens at P?
options: Partial interference, halfway between maximum and minimum
No interference, because the path difference is not zero
why: $1.5\lambda = (n + \tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$ with $n = 1$, so the waves arrive in antiphase and interfere destructively. Constructive needs a whole number of wavelengths.

q: In a double-slit experiment the slit separation is halved; nothing else changes. By what factor does the fringe separation change?
why: $s = \lambda D/d$, so $s$ is inversely proportional to $d$: halving $d$ doubles the fringe separation.

q: A diffraction grating has slit spacing $2.0\ \mu\text{m}$. The second-order maximum is at 30°. What is the wavelength in nm?
why: $n\lambda = d\sin\theta$: $\lambda = (2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.50)/2 = 5.0 \times 10^{-7}$ m $= 500$ nm.

q: Monochromatic light passes through a single slit. The slit is made narrower. How does the central maximum change?
why: $\theta = \lambda/b$, so a smaller $b$ spreads the central maximum wider. Less light gets through the narrower slit and it is spread out more, so it is dimmer.

q: On a standing wave of wavelength $\lambda$, what is the distance between two adjacent nodes?
why: Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart. $\lambda/4$ is the distance from a node to the next antinode.

q: A string 0.60 m long is fixed at both ends. Waves travel on it at $240\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. What is the frequency of the first harmonic in Hz?
why: The first harmonic has $\lambda = 2L = 1.20$ m, so $f = v/\lambda = 240/1.20 = 200$ Hz.

q: A pipe of length $L$ is closed at one end and open at the other. What is the wavelength of its first harmonic?
why: There is a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so $L = \lambda/4$ and $\lambda = 4L$. $2L$ is the answer for a pipe open at both ends.

q: What is the phase relationship between any two points on a standing wave that lie between the same pair of adjacent nodes?
options: Their phase difference increases steadily with their separation
why: All points between two adjacent nodes move up and down together, in phase, with different amplitudes. A steadily changing phase belongs to a travelling wave.

q: A pipe 0.85 m long is open at both ends. The speed of sound is $340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. What is the frequency of the third harmonic in Hz?
why: First harmonic: $\lambda = 2L = 1.70$ m, so $f_1 = 340/1.70 = 200$ Hz. The third harmonic is $3f_1 = 600$ Hz.

q: The damping of a driven oscillator is increased. What happens to its resonance peak?
options: Peak amplitude increases; resonant frequency shifts slightly higher
Peak amplitude stays the same; the peak becomes wider
Peak amplitude decreases; resonant frequency shifts slightly higher
Peak amplitude decreases; resonant frequency shifts slightly lower
why: More damping removes energy faster, so the maximum amplitude is smaller (and the peak broader). The resonant frequency moves slightly below the natural frequency.

q: A sound source moves towards a stationary observer. Compared with the emitted sound, what does the observer detect?
options: Higher frequency and the same wavelength
The same frequency and a shorter wavelength
why: The moving source bunches up the wavefronts ahead of it, so the wavelength is shorter and, at the same wave speed, the frequency is higher.

q: A spectral line emitted at 500.0 nm is observed from a galaxy at 505.0 nm. What is the galaxy's speed relative to us in $\text{km s}^{-1}$?
why: $v \approx c\,\Delta\lambda/\lambda = 3.00 \times 10^8 \times 5.0/500.0 = 3.0 \times 10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1} = 3000\ \text{km s}^{-1}$ (moving away, as it is a redshift).

q: The spectral lines from a distant galaxy are shifted to longer wavelengths. What does this tell us?
options: The galaxy is moving towards us
The galaxy is moving across our line of sight
The galaxy is moving away from us
why: A shift to longer wavelengths is a redshift, caused by the source and observer moving apart. Motion towards us would give a blueshift.

q: A wave source moves steadily to the right. What does its wavefront diagram look like?
options: Off-centre circles, crowded on the right
Off-centre circles, crowded on the left
Concentric circles, crowded on the right
why: Each wavefront is centred where the source was when it was emitted, so the centres shift right and the wavefronts crowd together ahead of the source.

q: A siren of frequency 500 Hz moves at $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ towards a stationary listener. Sound travels at $340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. What frequency, in Hz, is heard?
why: Moving source, approaching: $f' = f\,\dfrac{v}{v - u_s} = 500 \times \dfrac{340}{320} \approx 531$ Hz.

q: A listener moves at $34\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ away from a stationary 1000 Hz source. Sound travels at $340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. What frequency is heard?
why: Moving observer, receding: $f' = f\,\dfrac{v - u_o}{v} = 1000 \times \dfrac{306}{340} = 900$ Hz. 909 Hz comes from wrongly using the moving-source equation.
